chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Sprightly Tailor
chapters.artPrompt: a merry tailor sewing trews by candlelight on a flat gravestone inside a moonlit ruined church, a huge stone giant with a great head and shoulders slowly rising from the cracked floor, scattered thread and long stitches, scottish highland night, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago the great Macdonald lived in a castle at Saddell, by the western sea. He wanted a pair of trews, the fine old Highland clothes stitched all in one piece. "Make them for me by night in the old ruined church," said Macdonald. "Then you shall have a handsome reward." For that church was said to be haunted. Fearsome things walked there in the dark. The tailor was a sprightly man, which means merry and quick and brave. He was not to be daunted, and off he went up the glen when night came.

New word: trews — the old Highland dress of Scotland, coat and trousers stitched in one piece. It was trimmed with pretty fringes. It was warm for walking and grand for dancing. Only a very good tailor could sew a fine pair of trews.

He chose a flat gravestone for his seat, lighted his candle, put on his thimble, and began. All at once the floor trembled under his feet. A great head rose slowly up through the stone pavement. "Do you see this great head of mine?" thundered a mighty voice. "I see that, but I'll sew this!" said the tailor, and stitched away. Up rose the neck, the great chest, and two huge arms. "Do you see these great arms of mine?" "I see those, but I'll sew this!" said the tailor. And still he took longer and longer stitches.

Out came a great leg and stamped upon the pavement. "Do you see this great leg of mine?" "Aye, I see that, but I'll sew this!" cried the tailor. Just as the monster pulled up its other leg, the tailor finished the last stitch. He blew out his candle, sprang from the gravestone, and ran from the church with the trews under his arm. The fearsome thing roared and stamped and came after him down the glen. But the tailor had a nimble pair of legs and would not stop. He reached the castle gate, shut it behind him, and was safe.

The angry monster struck the wall above the gate, and left the mark of five great fingers there. Old people say the marks may be seen plainly to this day. As for the sprightly tailor, Macdonald paid him handsomely for the trews. Nobody ever noticed that a few of the stitches were rather long. So the brave man gained his reward, and the haunted church troubled honest folk no more.
The sprightly tailor stitches bravely while a great stone head rises from the church floor.

Saddell — a real castle on the west coast of Scotland, with an old abbey near it. Travelers there point out a stone wall above a gate. On it, they say, are the five great finger marks of the monster in this tale.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Munachar and Manachar
chapters.artPrompt: a thin lad with a basket standing at a raspberry bush while a greedy companion eats the berries behind his back, a cat, a cow, a hound and a deer watching from a grassy lane, sunny irish hedgerows, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago there lived two fellows, Munachar and Manachar, and a long time has passed since then. They went out together to pick raspberries. But as fast as Munachar picked, Manachar ate, till not a berry was left in the basket. "I must have a rod," said Munachar. "A gad, to punish Manachar who ate my raspberries, every one." He came to the rod. "You will not get me," said the rod, "until you get an axe to cut me."

New word: gad — a long slender twig, twisted and bent, that people once used for a switch. In old Ireland a gad was cut from a hazel rod by the roadside. It sounds a hard little word, but it was only a pliant twig.

He came to the axe. "You will not get me," said the axe. "Until you get a flag to edge me." He came to the flag. "You will not get me," said the flag. "Until you get water to wet me." The water wanted a deer to swim it. And the deer wanted a hound to hunt it. The hound wanted butter for his claw, and the butter wanted a cat to scrape it. The cat wanted milk, and the cow wanted a whisp of straw from the threshers. The threshers wanted the makings of a cake from the miller. And the miller wanted a full sieve of water from the river.

Munachar dipped the sieve in the river, but the water ran out as fast as he filled it. A crow flew over his head and cried, "Daub, daub!" "Good luck to you," said Munachar. "It is good advice you have." He daubed the sieve with red clay from the bank. Every hole was stopped, and the sieve held the water. Then the miller gave the makings of a cake. The threshers gave straw, the cow gave milk, the cat scraped the butter. The butter went into the hound's claw, the hound hunted the deer, the deer swam the water. The water wet the flag, and the flag edged the axe. The axe cut the rod, and the rod made the gad. And when Munachar had it ready at last, behold, Manachar had burst.
Munachar holds the leaking sieve while the crow cries its clever advice above him.

This merry tale is a chain story. Each new helper repeats the whole chain before him, and the string of names grows longer and longer. Long ago, people loved to chant such chains at the fireside, quicker and quicker, until everybody laughed.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · King O'Toole and His Goose
chapters.artPrompt: an old white bearded king by a green lake lifting his arms in wonder as a grey goose flies up strong and young, a gentle stranger in a dark cloak with one hand raised in blessing, round green hills of Ireland, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Far away and long ago there reigned a fine old king called O'Toole. He loved sport as he loved his life, and every morning he was away over the mountains after the deer. But in time the king grew old and stiff, and he could hunt no more. So he got a grey goose to cheer him. She swam the lake and dived for trout, and flew round and round to please him. Then the goose grew old, just like her master, and could divert him no longer.

One morning the king walked sadly by the lake, thinking of his cruel fate. Turning a corner, he met a decent young man who wished him good day. "How is your goose, King O'Toole?" asked the stranger. The king wondered how the fellow knew of his goose. "What is your trade?" said he. "I make old things as good as new," said the young man. "Then mend my old goose," cried the king, "and I will give you whatever you ask!"

"Then here is my bargain," said the stranger. "Give me all the ground the goose flies over," he said. "It must be the first offer, after I make her as good as new." "Honour bright!" said the king. They shook hands like two honest men. The saint took the old goose by the two wings, blessed her, and tossed her up in the air. Away she flew like an eagle, light as a lark, cutting capers in the sky. When she lit at his feet, the king patted her head for joy.

The king kept his word like a true man, and gave the saint the last acre he had. Then the stranger made himself known. "I am Saint Kavin," said the stranger. "I only came to try you." The king knelt down in wonder before the saint. The goose stayed young and strong as long as the king lived, and cheered him every day. And the ground the goose flew over was given to God's service, where a holy church rose among the hills.
The goose flies young and strong again while the old king and the disguised saint watch.

New word: Saint Kavin — an old Irish saint, better known as Saint Kevin. Long tales tell of his kindness to birds and beasts. In this story he comes in disguise, to try whether the old king keeps a true word.

Glendalough — a quiet valley in Ireland with two dark lakes, where Saint Kevin long ago made his home. Pilgrims still walk there among the round tower and the little stone churches. The valley keeps his name in every stone.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Jack and His Comrades
chapters.artPrompt: a farm boy, a grey donkey, a shaggy dog, a cat and a black cock stacked in a merry tower at a cottage window at night, candlelight and broken panes inside, frightened robbers fleeing to dark woods, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was once a poor widow who had one son called Jack. A hard summer came, and they did not know how they would live. "Bake my cake and kill my hen, mother," said Jack. "I will go seek my fortune." She gave him the whole cake with a thousand blessings. Then he set out at break of day. Soon he found a poor ass stuck to its shoulders in the bog. He piled in stones till the ass could climb out. Next he saved a dog from cruel boys who chased it. He fed a starving cat, and drove a fox away from a fine black cock. So Jack had four comrades, and they all went on together.

To seek your fortune — in the old tales this does not mean digging up treasure. It means walking out into the world to find work, luck, and friends. Jack carried only a cake and a kind heart, and that proved plenty.

When night came, they saw a light in a hollow, and heard singing and laughter inside. Jack crept to the window with his friends. Inside sat six fierce robbers feasting on roast beef and mulled beer. The robbers were boasting of a fine haul they had made at the Lord of Dunlavin's. Then Jack closed his ranks and gave the word of command. The ass stood at the window sill. The dog climbed on the ass's head, the cat on the dog's head. And the cock stood on top of all. At Jack's sign they all shouted together, "Hee-haw! Bow-wow! Meaw! Cock-a-doodle-doo!" The terrified robbers blew out the candles and fled away into the dark wood.

Jack and his party ate and drank and slept warm in the house. But the robbers in the cold wood grew vexed, and their captain crept back alone. The cat flew in his face, and the dog bit him. The cock clawed him, and the ass kicked him onto the dunghill. Off he limped to his men with a wild tale of a flax-carding hag, a cobbler, and a demon. Not one robber would go near that unlucky house again.

In the morning Jack packed the Lord of Dunlavin's gold and silver on the ass's back. The lord's rude porter tried to turn them away. Then the cock asked who had opened the door to the six robbers. "How did you know there were six?" stammered the porter, and his face went red as his frill. Then Jack was welcomed like a gentleman, dressed from top to toe, and made steward over all the lord's lands. He brought his mother to live near the castle. And the ass, dog, cat, and cock had the best places in the yard. And they were all as happy as you please.
The dog, cat, and cock pile on the ass's head at the robbers' window.

New word: steward — the trusted man who manages a great lord's house, farms, and money. A steward kept the keys and paid the workers, so the lord chose him with care. In the old days a poor boy with honest eyes could rise far.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Sea-Maiden
chapters.artPrompt: a young fisher lad on a small loch island with a black dog, a falcon and an otter beside him, a tiny silver egg lying on the sand, misty water and a distant maiden rising in the loch, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was once a poor old fisherman whose nets came up nearly empty. One day a sea-maiden rose beside his boat. "Plenty of fish I will send you," said the sea-maiden. "Give me your first son when he is twenty years old." The fisherman agreed at once. After that his boat was never empty. But as the twenty years drew to an end, he grew thin and sorrowful. His son made him tell the truth, and then the lad smiled. "Let not that trouble you. Make me a strong sword, and I will go seek my fortune."

Two swords snapped in his grip, but the third rang true. On his way he found a dog, a falcon, and an otter. They were quarrelling over a dead sheep, and he divided it fairly among them. Each promised to help him in his hour of need. He took service as a herd with a king, and found the cattle a green glen. A giant claimed the glen, but the lad's great sword swept once, and the giant fell. A second giant came raging, and the black dog gripped his neck till the herd struck him down. Then the lad fought a wicked old hag who kept a castle. With his dog's help he won her magic club. And after that there was peace on the hills.

Then came the darkest day. A three-headed beast in the loch demanded the king's daughter, and a boastful general hid in the rocks. The herd came in golden dress on the black horse and fought the beast three days running. Each day he cut off one head and gave it to the princess on a string. The general claimed the glory. But the princess spoke up for the true hero. "The man who took the heads from the knot has my ring," she said. "And he has my two earrings too." So the herd was known, and they were married that very day.

But on the very day his father had promised him, the sea-maiden rose and drew him down into the loch. His wife mourned by the water till an old wise man taught her. "Sea-maidens love music above everything," he said. So she played her harp on the shore, and the sea-maiden came up to listen. "Play on," said the sea-maiden. "Not till I see my man again," said the wife. Step by step, head and waist, she played her husband out of the loch. But the sea-maiden seized the wife in his place.

Then the old wise man told the husband the secret. The sea-maiden's soul was in an egg, in the mouth of a trout. The trout was in a hoodie, and the hoodie was in a hind. And the hind lived on an island in the middle of the loch. He leaped the strait on his black horse. The dog brought down the hind, the falcon struck the hoodie, and the otter brought the trout from the deep. Out dropped the little egg, and the husband set his foot upon it. "Break not the egg," cried the sea-maiden. "And you shall get all you ask." "Deliver to me my wife!" said he. The moment she was safe in his hands, he crushed the egg, and the sea-maiden was seen no more.
On the loch island the otter brings the trout that holds the little silver egg.

New word: sea-maiden — a maiden of the water in the old tales of Scotland and Ireland. She has a maid's face and voice, but she lives in the deep lochs. She loves music more than any other creature in the world.

New word: hoodie — a grey crow of the Scottish lochs, with a grey body and a dark hood. In the old tales a hoodie could change shape and carry a charm. Here the sea-maiden's life hides in a trout inside the hoodie.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Fair, Brown, and Trembling
chapters.artPrompt: a young woman in a gown white as snow riding a milk-white mare with a golden saddle past a stone church door, awestruck villagers and sisters shading their eyes, a small bird singing above the mare's ears, green irish countryside, celtic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago King Hugh Curucha lived in Tir Conal, and he had three daughters. Their names were Fair, and Brown, and Trembling. Fair and Brown had fine new dresses, and went to church every Sunday. Poor Trembling was kept at home to do the cooking and the work. Her sisters would not let her out of the house at all. For Trembling was more beautiful than both of them, and they were in dread she might marry first. Seven years went by in this way.

One Sunday morning the old henwife came into the kitchen. "It is at church you ought to be this day," said she. "How could I go, with no dress to wear?" asked Trembling. The henwife put on her cloak of darkness. She wished for the whitest robe in the world and green shoes. And there they stood before her that moment. She set a honey-bird on Trembling's right shoulder and a honey-finger on her left. At the door stood a milk-white mare with a golden saddle. "Do not go inside the church door," said the henwife. "When the people rise at the end of Mass, ride home before any man can stop you."

At the church door every eye turned to the wonderful lady, and no man knew who she was. When the people rose, she was away before the wind itself. The sisters came home full of the strange grand lady they had seen. On the second Sunday she wore black satin and red shoes, on a mare black and glossy. On the third Sunday her gown was red and white and green, and her golden hair flowed down. A bird sat between the mare's ears and sang all the way. This time the son of the king of Emania waited outside. He caught her by the foot, and ran beside the mare. The little shoe came off in his hand, and the lady was gone.

The prince kept the little shoe. He and all the princes rode through Erin to find the foot it fitted. Fair and Brown tried and tried, but it would fit neither of them. Then a voice called from the closet where they had locked Trembling. "There is another young woman in the house. I am here." The shoe fitted her exactly. She rode out in the three grand dresses. Every one cried, "That is the lady we saw at church." The prince fought for her and won her. And no man could claim her away. Then came the wedding, and it lasted a year and a day. So the kind youngest sister left the kitchen for ever.
Trembling rides the milk-white mare past the church door while every eye follows her.

New word: cloak of darkness — a magic hood in the old Irish tales. Whoever wore it could wish for robes, horses, or palaces, and see them stand ready at once. The henwife kept hers hidden, and used it here to help a hidden girl.

New word: henwife — the woman who kept the hens on a great farm long ago. She knew the hens' ways, the signs of weather, and a charm or two. In the old tales the henwife often knows more than she lets on.
